sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
UNSUPERVISED LEARNING - CLUSTERING ALGORITHMS

This module covers:
1. K-Means Clustering
2. Hierarchical Clustering
3. DBSCAN (Density-Based)
4. Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)

Each with:
- Visual Intuition
- Simple Explanation
- Real-world Use Cases
- Mathematical Foundation
- 3+ Code Examples
- Visualizations

Author: ML Learning Series
Module: 4/30

sections.title: Example 1: Basic K-Means
sections.body:
```python
print("Example 1: Basic K-Means (Customer Segmentation)")
print("-" * 60)

# Generate synthetic data (3 clear clusters)
np.random.seed(42)
X_kmeans, y_true = make_blobs(n_samples=300, centers=3, n_features=2,
                              cluster_std=0.6, random_state=42)

# Train K-Means
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
y_kmeans = kmeans.fit_predict(X_kmeans)

# Get cluster centers
centers = kmeans.cluster_centers_

# Calculate metrics
inertia = kmeans.inertia_
silhouette = silhouette_score(X_kmeans, y_kmeans)

print(f"Inertia (WCSS): {inertia:.2f}")
print(f"Silhouette Score: {silhouette:.4f} (Range: -1 to 1, higher better)")
print(f"Iterations to converge: {kmeans.n_iter_}")
print()

print("Cluster Centers:")
for i, center in enumerate(centers):
    print(f"  Cluster {i}: {center}")
print()

print("Cluster Sizes:")
unique, counts = np.unique(y_kmeans, return_counts=True)
for cluster, count in zip(unique, counts):
    print(f"  Cluster {cluster}: {count} points")
print()
```

sections.title: Example 2: Elbow Method (Finding Optimal K)
sections.body:
```python
print("Example 2: Elbow Method (Finding Optimal K)")
print("-" * 60)

# Try different K values
K_range = range(1, 11)
inertias = []
silhouette_scores = []

for k in K_range:
    kmeans_temp = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
    kmeans_temp.fit(X_kmeans)
    inertias.append(kmeans_temp.inertia_)
    
    if k > 1:  # Silhouette score needs at least 2 clusters
        silhouette_scores.append(silhouette_score(X_kmeans, kmeans_temp.labels_))
    else:
        silhouette_scores.append(0)

# Find elbow (using second derivative)
# Simple heuristic: maximum curvature
differences = np.diff(inertias)
differences2 = np.diff(differences)
elbow_k = np.argmax(np.abs(differences2)) + 2  # +2 because of two diffs

print("K vs Inertia:")
for k, inertia in zip(K_range, inertias):
    print(f"  K={k:2d}: Inertia={inertia:7.2f}")

print()
print(f"✓ Elbow Method suggests K = {elbow_k}")
print(f"✓ Best Silhouette Score at K = {K_range[np.argmax(silhouette_scores)]}")
print()
```

sections.title: Example 3: K-Means Limitations (Non-spherical clusters)
sections.body:
```python
print("Example 3: K-Means Limitations (Moon-shaped clusters)")
print("-" * 60)

# Generate non-spherical data
X_moons, y_moons_true = make_moons(n_samples=300, noise=0.05, random_state=42)

# Try K-Means
kmeans_moons = KMeans(n_clusters=2, init='k-means++', random_state=42)
y_moons_kmeans = kmeans_moons.fit_predict(X_moons)

silhouette_moons = silhouette_score(X_moons, y_moons_kmeans)

print(f"Silhouette Score on moon data: {silhouette_moons:.4f}")
print("✗ K-Means struggles with non-spherical clusters!")
print("  (We'll see DBSCAN handles this better)")
print()

"""
================================================================================
SECTION 2: HIERARCHICAL CLUSTERING
================================================================================

📊 VISUAL INTUITION:
-------------------
Hierarchical clustering builds a tree (dendrogram) of clusters:

Two approaches:
• Agglomerative (Bottom-up): Start with each point as cluster, merge similar ones
• Divisive (Top-down): Start with one cluster, split recursively

Think of family tree:
- Bottom-up: Individuals → Families → Clans → Tribes
- Top-down: Country → States → Cities → Neighborhoods

🎯 SIMPLE EXPLANATION:
----------------------
Agglomerative Algorithm:

1. Start: Each point is its own cluster (N clusters)
2. Repeat:
   a. Find two most similar clusters
   b. Merge them
3. Stop when K clusters remain (or all merged into 1)

Linkage methods (how to measure cluster similarity):
• Single: Closest points between clusters
• Complete: Farthest points between clusters
• Average: Average distance between all points
• Ward: Minimize variance (like K-Means)

🌍 REAL-WORLD USE CASES:
-------------------------
✓ Taxonomy: Species classification in biology
✓ Phylogenetics: Evolutionary trees
✓ Social Network Analysis: Community detection
✓ Document Organization: Topic hierarchies
✓ Gene Expression: Gene clustering in bioinformatics

🔑 KEY CONCEPTS:
----------------
1. **Dendrogram**: Tree showing merge history
   • Height = dissimilarity when merged
   • Cut at desired level → K clusters

2. **Linkage Methods**:
   • Single: Sensitive to noise (chaining effect)
   • Complete: Produces compact clusters
   • Average: Balance between single/complete
   • Ward: Minimizes variance (most popular)

3. **Distance Metrics**:
   • Euclidean (most common)
   • Manhattan, Cosine, etc.

4. **No Need to Specify K**: Cut dendrogram at desired level!

5. **Advantages**:
   ✓ Hierarchical structure (interpretable!)
   ✓ Don't need to specify K
   ✓ Deterministic (no random initialization)
   ✓ Works with any distance metric
   
6. **Disadvantages**:
   ✗ Slow for large datasets (O(n³) or O(n²log n))
   ✗ Can't undo merges
   ✗ Sensitive to outliers

📐 MATHEMATICAL FOUNDATION:
---------------------------
Distance between clusters C₁ and C₂:

Single Linkage:
    d(C₁, C₂) = min{d(x, y) : x ∈ C₁, y ∈ C₂}

Complete Linkage:
    d(C₁, C₂) = max{d(x, y) : x ∈ C₁, y ∈ C₂}

Average Linkage:
    d(C₁, C₂) = (1/(|C₁||C₂|)) Σₓ∈C₁ Σᵧ∈C₂ d(x, y)

Ward's Method:
    Merge clusters that minimize increase in total within-cluster variance
"""

print("=" * 80)
print("SECTION 2: HIERARCHICAL CLUSTERING")
print("=" * 80)
print()
```

sections.title: Example 2: Different Linkage Methods
sections.body:
```python
print("Example 2: Comparing Linkage Methods")
print("-" * 60)

linkage_methods = ['single', 'complete', 'average', 'ward']
linkage_results = {}

for method in linkage_methods:
    hierarchical_temp = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage=method)
    labels = hierarchical_temp.fit_predict(X_kmeans)
    score = silhouette_score(X_kmeans, labels)
    linkage_results[method] = (labels, score)
    
    print(f"{method.capitalize():10s} linkage: Silhouette = {score:.4f}")

print()
best_linkage = max(linkage_results.items(), key=lambda x: x[1][1])[0]
print(f"✓ Best linkage method: {best_linkage} (highest silhouette)")
print()
```

```python
"""
================================================================================
SECTION 3: DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering)
================================================================================

📊 VISUAL INTUITION:
-------------------
DBSCAN finds clusters based on density:

Think of it like finding crowds in a park:
- Dense areas (many people close together) = clusters
- Sparse areas (few people spread out) = noise/outliers
- Can find crowds of any shape!

Key idea: Clusters = regions of high density separated by regions of low density

🎯 SIMPLE EXPLANATION:
----------------------
DBSCAN algorithm:

1. Pick a point
2. Find all points within ε (epsilon) distance
3. If ≥ min_samples points nearby:
   • Core point → Start cluster
   • Expand cluster to include all reachable points
4. If < min_samples nearby:
   • Border point or noise
5. Repeat for all unvisited points

Result: Arbitrary-shaped clusters + noise points!

🌍 REAL-WORLD USE CASES:
-------------------------
✓ Anomaly Detection: Noise points = outliers
✓ Geographic Clustering: City neighborhoods, crime hotspots
✓ Image Segmentation: Group similar pixel regions
✓ Astronomy: Galaxy clustering
✓ Traffic Analysis: Congestion detection

🔑 KEY CONCEPTS:
----------------
1. **Core Point**: Has ≥ min_samples within ε distance
   • Forms the "core" of a cluster

2. **Border Point**: Within ε of core point, but not core itself
   • On edge of cluster

3. **Noise Point**: Not core, not border
   • Outliers!

4. **Parameters**:
   • ε (eps): Neighborhood radius
   • min_samples: Minimum points to form dense region

5. **Advantages**:
   ✓ Finds arbitrary-shaped clusters (not just spherical!)
   ✓ Identifies outliers (noise points)
   ✓ Don't need to specify K
   ✓ Robust to outliers
   
6. **Disadvantages**:
   ✗ Sensitive to ε and min_samples
   ✗ Struggles with varying densities
   ✗ High-dimensional data (curse of dimensionality)

📐 MATHEMATICAL FOUNDATION:
---------------------------
Definitions:

ε-neighborhood of point p:
    Nₑ(p) = {q : d(p, q) ≤ ε}

Core point:
    |Nₑ(p)| ≥ min_samples

Directly density-reachable:
    q ∈ Nₑ(p) and p is core point

Density-reachable (transitive):
    Chain of directly density-reachable points

Cluster:
    Maximal set of density-reachable points
"""

print("=" * 80)
print("SECTION 3: DBSCAN (DENSITY-BASED CLUSTERING)")
print("=" * 80)
print()
```

sections.title: Example 1: Dbscan on Moon-shaped Data
sections.body:
```python
print("Example 1: DBSCAN on Non-spherical Clusters")
print("-" * 60)

# Use moon data (where K-Means failed)
dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=0.3, min_samples=5)
y_dbscan = dbscan.fit_predict(X_moons)

# Count clusters (excluding noise which is labeled -1)
n_clusters_dbscan = len(set(y_dbscan)) - (1 if -1 in y_dbscan else 0)
n_noise = list(y_dbscan).count(-1)

print(f"Number of clusters: {n_clusters_dbscan}")
print(f"Number of noise points: {n_noise}")
print()

# Calculate silhouette (excluding noise)
if n_clusters_dbscan > 1:
    mask = y_dbscan != -1
    if np.sum(mask) > 0:
        silhouette_dbscan = silhouette_score(X_moons[mask], y_dbscan[mask])
        print(f"Silhouette Score: {silhouette_dbscan:.4f}")
        print("✓ DBSCAN handles non-spherical clusters well!")
print()
```

sections.title: Example 3: Dbscan for Outlier Detection
sections.body:
```python
print("Example 3: Outlier Detection with DBSCAN")
print("-" * 60)

# Generate data with outliers
np.random.seed(42)
X_outliers = np.concatenate([
    np.random.randn(200, 2) * 0.5,  # Main cluster
    np.random.randn(10, 2) * 0.3 + [4, 4]  # Outliers
])

# Apply DBSCAN
dbscan_outlier = DBSCAN(eps=0.5, min_samples=5)
labels_outlier = dbscan_outlier.fit_predict(X_outliers)

n_outliers = list(labels_outlier).count(-1)
print(f"Detected outliers: {n_outliers}/210 points")
print(f"Outlier percentage: {n_outliers/210*100:.1f}%")
print("✓ DBSCAN excellent for anomaly detection!")
print()

"""
================================================================================
SECTION 4: GAUSSIAN MIXTURE MODELS (GMM)
================================================================================

📊 VISUAL INTUITION:
-------------------
GMM assumes data comes from mixture of Gaussian distributions:

Think of heights in a population:
- Women's heights ~ Normal(μ₁, σ₁)
- Men's heights ~ Normal(μ₂, σ₂)
- Overall population = mixture of both!

GMM finds:
• How many Gaussians (K)
• Parameters of each (μ, σ)
• Mixing proportions (π)

🎯 SIMPLE EXPLANATION:
----------------------
GMM is "soft clustering":
• K-Means: Each point belongs to ONE cluster (hard)
• GMM: Each point has PROBABILITY of belonging to each cluster (soft)

Example:
• K-Means: "This customer is in segment 2"
• GMM: "This customer is 70% segment 2, 30% segment 1"

Fitted using EM (Expectation-Maximization) algorithm

🌍 REAL-WORLD USE CASES:
-------------------------
✓ Image Segmentation: Probabilistic pixel classification
✓ Speaker Recognition: Voice pattern modeling
✓ Anomaly Detection: Points with low probability = outliers
✓ Financial Modeling: Asset return distributions
✓ Bioinformatics: Gene expression patterns

🔑 KEY CONCEPTS:
----------------
1. **Soft Clustering**: Probabilistic assignments
   • Each point: probability distribution over clusters

2. **Model Components**:
   • μₖ: Mean of Gaussian k
   • Σₖ: Covariance of Gaussian k
   • πₖ: Mixing coefficient (prior probability)

3. **EM Algorithm**:
   • E-step: Compute cluster responsibilities
   • M-step: Update parameters
   • Repeat until convergence

4. **Covariance Types**:
   • Full: Each cluster has full covariance matrix
   • Tied: All clusters share same covariance
   • Diag: Diagonal covariance (axes-aligned ellipses)
   • Spherical: σ²I (circles, like K-Means)

5. **Advantages**:
   ✓ Soft clustering (probabilities)
   ✓ Handles elliptical clusters
   ✓ Theoretically principled (probability model)
   ✓ Can estimate density
   
6. **Disadvantages**:
   ✗ Sensitive to initialization
   ✗ Can converge to local optima
   ✗ Need to choose K

📐 MATHEMATICAL FOUNDATION:
---------------------------
Model:
    p(x) = Σₖ πₖ · N(x | μₖ, Σₖ)

where:
- πₖ = mixing coefficient (Σπₖ = 1)
- N(x | μₖ, Σₖ) = Gaussian with mean μₖ, covariance Σₖ

Gaussian density:
    N(x | μ, Σ) = (1/((2π)^(d/2)|Σ|^(1/2))) exp(-1/2(x-μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x-μ))

Responsibility (probability point i belongs to cluster k):
    γᵢₖ = πₖN(xᵢ|μₖ,Σₖ) / Σⱼ πⱼN(xᵢ|μⱼ,Σⱼ)

EM updates:
    μₖ = (1/Nₖ)Σᵢ γᵢₖxᵢ
    Σₖ = (1/Nₖ)Σᵢ γᵢₖ(xᵢ-μₖ)(xᵢ-μₖ)ᵀ
    πₖ = Nₖ/N
"""

print("=" * 80)
print("SECTION 4: GAUSSIAN MIXTURE MODELS (GMM)")
print("=" * 80)
print()
```

sections.title: Example 1: Gmm vs K-Means
sections.body:
```python
print("Example 1: GMM vs K-Means (Soft vs Hard Clustering)")
print("-" * 60)

# Train GMM
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, random_state=42)
gmm.fit(X_kmeans)
y_gmm = gmm.predict(X_kmeans)
proba_gmm = gmm.predict_proba(X_kmeans)

# Compare with K-Means
silhouette_gmm = silhouette_score(X_kmeans, y_gmm)

print("K-Means:")
print(f"  Silhouette Score: {silhouette:.4f}")
print("  Hard assignment: Each point → 1 cluster")
print()

print("GMM:")
print(f"  Silhouette Score: {silhouette_gmm:.4f}")
print("  Soft assignment: Each point → probability distribution")
print()

print("Sample GMM Probabilities (first 3 points):")
for i in range(3):
    print(f"  Point {i}: Cluster 0={proba_gmm[i,0]:.3f}, "
          f"Cluster 1={proba_gmm[i,1]:.3f}, Cluster 2={proba_gmm[i,2]:.3f}")
print()
```

sections.title: Example 2: Choosing Number of Components (Bic/Aic)
sections.body:
```python
print("Example 2: Model Selection with BIC/AIC")
print("-" * 60)

n_components_range = range(1, 8)
bic_scores = []
aic_scores = []

for n in n_components_range:
    gmm_temp = GaussianMixture(n_components=n, random_state=42)
    gmm_temp.fit(X_kmeans)
    bic_scores.append(gmm_temp.bic(X_kmeans))
    aic_scores.append(gmm_temp.aic(X_kmeans))

optimal_bic = n_components_range[np.argmin(bic_scores)]
optimal_aic = n_components_range[np.argmin(aic_scores)]

print(f"{'K':<5} {'BIC':<12} {'AIC':<12}")
print("-" * 30)
for n, bic, aic in zip(n_components_range, bic_scores, aic_scores):
    marker_bic = " ← Best" if n == optimal_bic else ""
    marker_aic = " ← Best" if n == optimal_aic else ""
    print(f"{n:<5} {bic:<12.2f}{marker_bic} {aic:<12.2f}{marker_aic}")

print()
print(f"✓ BIC suggests K = {optimal_bic} (lower is better)")
print(f"✓ AIC suggests K = {optimal_aic} (lower is better)")
print()
```

sections.title: Example 3: Gmm for Anomaly Detection
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Points with very low likelihood = anomalies
- Row 2: Hierarchical & DBSCAN
- Row 3: GMM and Comparisons

```python
print("Example 3: Anomaly Detection with GMM")
print("-" * 60)

# Fit GMM
gmm_anomaly = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, random_state=42)
gmm_anomaly.fit(X_kmeans)

# Get log-likelihood (score_samples)
log_likelihood = gmm_anomaly.score_samples(X_kmeans)

# Points with very low likelihood = anomalies
threshold = np.percentile(log_likelihood, 5)  # Bottom 5%
anomalies = log_likelihood < threshold

n_anomalies = np.sum(anomalies)
print(f"Detected anomalies: {n_anomalies}/{len(X_kmeans)} points")
print(f"Threshold (log-likelihood): {threshold:.2f}")
print()

print("Sample log-likelihoods:")
print(f"  Normal points: {log_likelihood[~anomalies][:3]}")
print(f"  Anomalies: {log_likelihood[anomalies][:3]}")
print()
print("✓ Lower log-likelihood = less likely to belong to any cluster = anomaly!")
print()

# Comprehensive Visualization
print("Creating comprehensive clustering visualizations...")

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(18, 14))

# Row 1: K-Means
ax1 = plt.subplot(3, 3, 1)
scatter1 = ax1.scatter(X_kmeans[:, 0], X_kmeans[:, 1], c=y_kmeans, cmap='viridis', s=50, alpha=0.6)
ax1.scatter(centers[:, 0], centers[:, 1], c='red', marker='X', s=300, edgecolors='black', linewidth=2, label='Centroids')
ax1.set_title(f'K-Means Clustering\nSilhouette={silhouette:.3f}', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax1.legend()
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

ax2 = plt.subplot(3, 3, 2)
ax2.plot(K_range, inertias, 'o-', linewidth=2, markersize=8)
ax2.axvline(x=elbow_k, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=2, label=f'Elbow K={elbow_k}')
ax2.set_xlabel('Number of Clusters (K)')
ax2.set_ylabel('Inertia (WCSS)')
ax2.set_title('Elbow Method\n(Find optimal K)', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax2.legend()
ax2.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

ax3 = plt.subplot(3, 3, 3)
ax3.scatter(X_moons[:, 0], X_moons[:, 1], c=y_moons_kmeans, cmap='viridis', s=50, alpha=0.6)
ax3.set_title(f'K-Means on Moons\n(Fails on non-spherical)', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax3.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Row 2: Hierarchical & DBSCAN
ax4 = plt.subplot(3, 3, 4)
ax4.scatter(X_kmeans[:, 0], X_kmeans[:, 1], c=y_hierarchical, cmap='viridis', s=50, alpha=0.6)
ax4.set_title(f'Hierarchical Clustering\nSilhouette={silhouette_hier:.3f}', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax4.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

ax5 = plt.subplot(3, 3, 5)
dendrogram(linkage_matrix, ax=ax5, truncate_mode='lastp', p=12, leaf_rotation=90)
ax5.set_xlabel('Cluster Size')
ax5.set_ylabel('Distance')
ax5.set_title('Dendrogram\n(Hierarchical structure)', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')

ax6 = plt.subplot(3, 3, 6)
scatter6 = ax6.scatter(X_moons[:, 0], X_moons[:, 1], c=y_dbscan, cmap='viridis', s=50, alpha=0.6)
# Highlight noise points
noise_mask = y_dbscan == -1
ax6.scatter(X_moons[noise_mask, 0], X_moons[noise_mask, 1], c='red', marker='x', s=100, label='Noise', linewidth=2)
ax6.set_title(f'DBSCAN on Moons\n(Handles non-spherical!)', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax6.legend()
ax6.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Row 3: GMM and Comparisons
ax7 = plt.subplot(3, 3, 7)
ax7.scatter(X_kmeans[:, 0], X_kmeans[:, 1], c=y_gmm, cmap='viridis', s=50, alpha=0.6)

# Plot GMM ellipses
from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse
for i in range(gmm.n_components):
    mean = gmm.means_[i]
    covar = gmm.covariances_[i]
    
    # Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
    v, w = np.linalg.eigh(covar)
    v = 2. * np.sqrt(2.) * np.sqrt(v)
    u = w[0] / np.linalg.norm(w[0])
    
    # Calculate angle
    angle = np.arctan(u[1] / u[0])
    angle = 180. * angle / np.pi
    
    ell = Ellipse(mean, v[0], v[1], angle=180. + angle, color='red', alpha=0.3, linewidth=2)
    ax7.add_patch(ell)

ax7.set_title(f'GMM (Soft Clustering)\nSilhouette={silhouette_gmm:.3f}', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax7.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

ax8 = plt.subplot(3, 3, 8)
ax8.plot(n_components_range, bic_scores, 'o-', linewidth=2, label='BIC', markersize=8)
ax8.plot(n_components_range, aic_scores, 's-', linewidth=2, label='AIC', markersize=8)
ax8.axvline(x=optimal_bic, color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
ax8.set_xlabel('Number of Components')
ax8.set_ylabel('Information Criterion')
ax8.set_title('GMM Model Selection\n(Lower is better)', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax8.legend()

ax9 = plt.subplot(3, 3, 9)
```
